_comment: Short facts taken from the chapter the day page reads (CPDV). Keyed by book:chapter so the section stays with the reading, not a stale date.

items: Joseph brings his sons Manasseh and Ephraim to Jacob when he hears that his father is sick.
Jacob crosses his hands: the right hand rests on Ephraim, the younger, and the left on Manasseh, the elder.
Joseph tries to move the right hand onto the firstborn. Jacob refuses, and he sets Ephraim ahead of Manasseh.
Jacob calls his sons and speaks a word over each of the twelve.
Reuben, the firstborn, is called the beginning of his sorrow. Simeon and Levi are divided because of their violence.
Of Judah he says the scepter will not be taken away until the one who will be sent arrives, the expectation of the Gentiles.
Jacob is carried to Canaan and buried in the double cave Abraham bought from Ephron the Hittite, opposite Mamre.
Joseph tells his brothers, “You devised evil against me. But God turned it into good,” so that many peoples would be saved.
Before he dies, Joseph makes the sons of Israel swear to carry his bones with them when God visits them.
A new king arises over Egypt who is ignorant of Joseph.
The Hebrew midwives are named Shiphrah and Puah. They fear God and let the boys live.
Pharaoh then orders every newborn Hebrew son to be thrown into the river.
When his mother can no longer hide him, she lays Moses in a basket of bulrushes smeared with pitch and tar.
Pharaoh’s daughter finds the basket among the papyruses. Moses later flees to Midian and marries Zipporah.
Their son is named Gershom, “for I have been a newcomer in a foreign land.”
The Lord appears to Moses in a flame of fire from the midst of a bush that burns and is not burnt.
He calls, “Moses, Moses,” and says he is the God of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. Moses hides his face.
When Moses asks his name, God says, “I AM WHO AM,” and tells him to say, “HE WHO IS has sent me to you.”
Moses says he is not eloquent. The Lord gives him Aaron, his brother, to speak for him.
On the way, Zipporah circumcises their son with a sharp stone and says, “You are a bloody spouse to me.”
Aaron meets Moses. They gather the elders, Aaron speaks the words of the Lord, and the people believe.
Moses and Aaron tell Pharaoh that the Lord says, “Release my people.” Pharaoh answers that he does not know the Lord.
The king stops giving chaff for the bricks and still demands the same quota. The people have to gather straw themselves.
The foremen are scourged for missing the quota. They tell Moses and Aaron, “You have caused our odor to become foul before Pharaoh.”
The Lord tells Moses, “I am the Lord,” and says he has remembered his covenant with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
He promises to lead Israel out from the work house of the Egyptians and to take them as his people.
Moses explains this to the sons of Israel. They do not agree with him, because of their anguish of spirit and very difficult work.
Aaron’s staff becomes a serpent and devours the staffs of Pharaoh’s sorcerers.
The water of the river is struck and turned into blood. The fish die, and the Egyptians cannot drink it.
The sorcerers do the same by their incantations. Seven days pass after the Lord strikes the river.
Frogs come up into the houses, bedrooms, beds, and ovens. Pharaoh begs for them to be taken away, then hardens his heart.
The sorcerers cannot bring forth the gnats and say, “This is the finger of God.”
Flies fill Egypt, but the land of Goshen, where the Lord’s people live, is spared.
Hail and fire fall on Egypt, greater than any since the nation was formed. Goshen is left untouched.
Moses stretches out his hands and the thunder and hail cease.
When Pharaoh sees that they have stopped, he adds to his sin and will not let the people go.
Locusts eat whatever the hail left. A west wind then casts them into the Red Sea, and not one remains.
Moses stretches out his hand and a darkness that can be felt covers Egypt for three days.
The sons of Israel have light where they live. Moses says not one hoof of the flocks will stay behind, because the animals are needed for the worship of the Lord.
There is one plague left. After it, Pharaoh will not merely let the people go. He will drive them out.
Every firstborn in Egypt will die, from Pharaoh’s firstborn on the throne to the firstborn of the handmaid at the millstone, and the firstborn of the cattle.
Moses goes out from Pharaoh exceedingly angry. Among the sons of Israel, not even a dog will mutter.
The Passover lamb is eaten in haste, with waist girded, shoes on, and a staff in hand. It is the Lord’s Passover.
At midnight the Lord strikes every firstborn in Egypt, from Pharaoh’s heir to the captive in prison, and every firstborn of the cattle.
Israel had lived in Egypt four hundred and thirty years. On that same day the army of the Lord departs.
Every firstborn that opens the womb, of men and of cattle, is to be sanctified to the Lord.
God does not lead them by the way of the Philistines. He leads them around by the desert next to the Red Sea.
Moses carries the bones of Joseph, as Joseph had made Israel swear. The Lord goes before them in a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night.
Moses tells the people, “The Lord will fight on your behalf, and you will remain silent.”
Israel goes through the midst of the dried sea, with the water like a wall on the right and on the left.
The waters return over Pharaoh’s chariots and horsemen. Not one of the army that followed them into the sea is left.
Moses and the sons of Israel sing, “The horse and the rider he has cast into the sea.” Miriam takes a timbrel and leads the women.
At Marah the water is bitter. The Lord shows Moses a tree, and the water becomes sweet.
At Elim there are twelve fountains of water and seventy palm trees, and they camp beside the waters.
The Lord rains bread from heaven and tells them to gather only enough for each day, as a test.
On the sixth day they collect a double portion, two omers for each man, because the next day is the Sabbath rest.
Aaron stores one omer of manna in a vessel, kept in the sight of the Lord for the generations to come.
At Rephidim there is no water. Moses strikes the rock at Horeb and water comes out for the people to drink.
Amalek fights Israel there. When Moses lifts his hands, Israel prevails. When he lowers them, Amalek prevails.
Aaron and Hur hold up his hands until sunset. Moses builds an altar and names it “The Lord, my Exaltation.”
Jethro, the priest of Midian and kinsman of Moses, brings Zipporah and their two sons, Gershom and Eliezer, to the wilderness.
Jethro rejoices over all the good the Lord has done for Israel, and he offers holocausts and sacrifices to God.
He tells Moses to appoint capable men who fear God, love truth, and hate avarice, as tribunes and leaders of hundreds, fifties, and tens.
In the third month after leaving Egypt, Israel camps in the wilderness of Sinai, and Moses goes up to God.
The Lord says that if they keep his covenant they will be “a priestly kingdom and a holy nation.” The people answer, “Everything that the Lord has spoken, we shall do.”
On the third day the Lord descends on Mount Sinai in fire. The mountain smokes like a furnace, and the trumpet grows louder while Moses speaks and God answers.
The Lord says, “I am the Lord your God, who led you away from the land of Egypt, out of the house of servitude,” and “You shall not have strange gods before me.”
He tells them to sanctify the Sabbath, because in six days the Lord made heaven and earth and the sea, and he rested on the seventh day.
The people stand far off in fear and ask Moses to speak to them. Moses draws near to the mist where God is.
A Hebrew servant serves six years and departs free in the seventh. If he says he loves his lord, his wife, and his children, his ear is pierced with an awl and he remains.
Whoever strikes a man intending to murder, or strikes his father or mother, or steals a man and sells him, shall be put to death.
If a quarrel ends in the death of a pregnant woman, the judgment is a life for a life, an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth, a hand for a hand, and a foot for a foot.
Someone who steals an ox or a sheep and then kills or sells it restores five oxen for the ox and four sheep for the sheep. If the animal is found alive, he repays double.
“You shall not harass the newcomer, nor shall you afflict him,” because Israel was once newcomers in Egypt, and “You shall not harm a widow or an orphan.”
A garment taken as a pledge is returned before sunset, because it is the neighbor’s only covering for the night. Tithes and first-fruits are not to be delayed.
“You shall not follow the crowd in doing evil,” nor agree with the majority apart from the truth, and you shall not take bribes, which blind even the prudent.
An enemy’s stray ox or donkey is led back to him. If the donkey of someone who hates you has fallen under its burden, you lift it up with him.
Three times a year every male appears before the Lord. The Lord will send his Angel ahead, and he says, “You shall not cook a young goat in the milk of its mother.”
Moses reads the book of the covenant. The people answer, “All that the Lord has spoken, we will do, and we will be obedient.” He sprinkles the blood and says, “This is the blood of the covenant.”
Moses, Aaron, Nadab, Abihu, and seventy elders go up. They see the God of Israel, and under his feet is something like a work of sapphire stone. They eat and drink.
A cloud covers Sinai for six days. On the seventh day the Lord calls Moses from the middle of the mist. Moses stays on the mountain forty days and forty nights.
The ark of setim wood is two and one half cubits long, and one and one half cubits wide and high. It is overlaid with gold. The bars stay in the rings and are never drawn out.
Two cherubim of formed gold spread their wings over the propitiatory, faces turned toward it. The Lord says he will speak from there, between the two cherubim.
The lampstand is formed from the finest gold, with six branches and seven lamps. Its whole weight is one talent of gold, made according to the example shown on the mountain.
Ten curtains of fine twisted linen, hyacinth, purple, and twice-dyed scarlet are coupled five and five. Fifty gold rings join them so that it is one tabernacle.
Eleven haircloth canopies cover the roof, then skins of rams dyed red, and above those violet-colored skins. The standing panels are setim wood, overlaid with gold.

A veil before four columns divides the Sanctuary from the Sanctuary of Sanctuaries. The ark and the propitiatory are beyond the veil. The table stands outside it, and the lampstand stands opposite the table.

The altar of setim wood is five cubits on each side and three cubits high, with horns at the four corners, and it is covered with brass. It is empty and hollow inside, as it was shown on the mountain.
The atrium is one hundred cubits long and fifty wide, hung with fine twisted linen. Its columns have bases of brass, and the embroidered hanging at the entrance is twenty cubits.
The sons of Israel bring the purest oil of the olive trees, crushed with a pestle, so that a lamp may always burn outside the veil. Aaron and his sons arrange it until morning.

Aaron, with Nadab, Abihu, Eleazar, and Ithamar, is set apart to exercise the priesthood. The holy vestments are a breastplate, an ephod, a tunic, a close-fit linen garment, a headdress, and a wide belt.

Two onyx stones are engraved with the names of the sons of Israel, six on each, and Aaron carries them on both shoulders. The breastplate of judgment has twelve stones, one name for each tribe, and Doctrine and Truth are placed in it.
The tunic’s hem has pomegranates and golden bells, so the sound is heard when Aaron enters and leaves the Sanctuary. A plate of gold on the headdress is engraved, “Holy to the Lord.”
Aaron and his sons lay their hands on the ram of consecration. Its blood is put on the tip of the right ear and on the thumbs and big toes of the right hand and the right foot.
They eat its flesh and the unleavened bread in the vestibule of the tabernacle. A stranger shall not eat from these. Whatever remains until morning is burned with fire.
Their hands are consecrated for seven days. One lamb is offered in the morning and another in the evening. The Lord says, “I will live in the midst of the sons of Israel, and I will be their God.”

The altar for burning incense is one cubit square and two cubits high, set opposite the veil. Aaron burns incense on it morning and evening. Once a year he makes atonement on its horns with the blood of the sin offering.
Everyone numbered from twenty years and above gives half a shekel as a price for their souls. A shekel is twenty obols. The rich do not add to the half shekel, and the poor do not give less.

The holy oil of unction is the best myrrh, cinnamon, sweet flag, cassia, and olive oil. The incense is stacte, onycha, galbanum, and frankincense in equal weight. Neither one is to be copied for ordinary use.
The Lord calls Bezalel, the son of Uri, the son of Hur, from the tribe of Judah, by name, and fills him with the Spirit of God, with wisdom, understanding, and knowledge in every craft.
Oholiab, the son of Ahisamach, from the tribe of Dan, is given as his associate, and wisdom is placed in the heart of every artisan who will make the tabernacle.

The Sabbath is a sign between the Lord and the sons of Israel, for in six days the Lord made heaven and earth, and on the seventh he ceased from work. He then gives Moses two stone tablets of testimony, written with the finger of God.

The people tell Aaron, “Rise up, make us gods, who may go before us.” From their golden earrings he makes a molten calf, and they say, “These are your gods, O Israel, who led you away from the land of Egypt.”

Moses begs the Lord to remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel. The Lord is appeased from the evil he had spoken. Moses then breaks the tablets at the base of the mountain, burns the calf, and grinds it even to dust.

The sons of Levi gather to Moses, and about twenty-three thousand men fall that day. Moses says, “Either release them from this offense, or, if you do not, then delete me from the book that you have written.”

The Lord tells Moses to go up to the land sworn to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, but says, “For I will not go up with you, since you are a stiff-necked people,” lest he destroy them on the way. The people mourn and put aside their ornaments before Mount Horeb.
Moses pitches the Tabernacle of the Covenant beyond the camp. The pillar of cloud stands at the door, and the Lord speaks to Moses face to face, as a man speaks to his friend.
Moses says, “Show me your glory.” The Lord answers, “You are not able to see my face. For man shall not see me and live.” He sets Moses in a cleft of the rock until his glory passes by.

Moses cuts two stone tablets like the first. The Lord descends in a cloud and says, “The Ruler, the Lord God, merciful and lenient, patient and full of compassion and also truthful,” who preserves mercy a thousand fold.

Israel is told not to make molten gods, to keep the solemnity of unleavened bread, and, “You shall not boil a young goat in the milk of its mother.” Moses stays forty days and forty nights and writes the ten words of the covenant.

When he descends, he does not know that his face is radiant. Aaron and the sons of Israel are afraid to approach, so he places a veil over his face and takes it off when he goes in to speak with the Lord.
Moses tells the gathered sons of Israel to work six days and to keep the seventh as the Sabbath, and, “You shall not kindle a fire in any of your dwelling places throughout the day of the Sabbath.”
Everyone with a ready soul offers gold, fabric, skins, and setim wood. The skillful women spin hyacinth, purple, vermillion, and fine linen, and give the hair of goats of their own accord.
Moses says the Lord has called Bezalel of Judah by name and filled him with the Spirit of God, and has given the same wisdom to Oholiab of Dan, to make the work of the tabernacle.

Bezalel, Oholiab, and every wise man make what the Sanctuary needs. The people offer more than is needed, so Moses proclaims, “Let neither man nor woman offer anything further for the work of the Sanctuary.”
They make ten curtains of fine twisted linen, each twenty-eight cubits by four, joined by fifty gold rings, and eleven canopies from the hair of goats to cover the roof.
They make the standing panels of setim wood, overlay them with gold, hang the veil of hyacinth, purple, vermillion, and fine linen, and set five columns at the entrance.
Bezalel makes the ark of setim wood, two and one half cubits long and one and one half cubits wide and high, clothed with the purest gold, and two Cherubim of ductile gold over the propitiatory.
He makes the table and its vessels of pure gold, and the lampstand with seven lamps. The lampstand with all its vessels weighs a talent of gold.
He makes the altar of incense, one cubit on each side and two cubits high, clothed with gold, and he composes the oil for the ointment of sanctification and the incense with the skill of a perfumer.

The altar of holocaust is five cubits square and three cubits high, covered with brass, hollow and made from panels. The washtub of brass and its base are made from the mirrors of the women who kept watch at the door of the tabernacle.

Bezalel, the son of Uri, the son of Hur, from the tribe of Judah, completes the work as the Lord decreed through Moses, joined by Oholiab of Dan. Ithamar, the son of Aaron, enumerates the instruments with the Levites.

The gold expended in the Sanctuary is twenty-nine talents and seven hundred thirty shekels, offered by six hundred and three thousand, five hundred and fifty men able to bear arms, from twenty years and above.
The ephod is woven with gold threads cut and drawn into the colors, and two onyx stones are engraved with the names of the sons of Israel and set in its sides.

The breastplate has four rows of gems, twelve stones engraved with the names of the twelve tribes. The plate of sacred veneration reads “Holy to the Lord.” The hem of the tunic carries gold bells and pomegranates.
The sons of Israel offer the finished tabernacle and every article commanded for its ministry. Moses sees that everything is completed, and he blesses them.
On the first day of the first month, Moses raises the tabernacle, places the testimony in the ark, draws the veil before it, and sets the bread of the presence and the seven lamps in order.
He anoints the tabernacle and its vessels with the oil of unction, washes Aaron and his sons, and clothes them in the holy vestments so that their unction may accomplish an everlasting priesthood.

The cloud covers the tabernacle of the testimony, and the glory of the Lord fills it, so that Moses cannot enter. When the cloud departs, the sons of Israel set out. The cloud is over it by day, and the fire by night.
The Lord calls Moses and speaks from the tabernacle of the testimony. A holocaust from the herd is an immaculate male at the door of the tabernacle.
The one who offers places his hand on the head of the sacrifice, so that it is acceptable for expiation. The priests pour its blood around the altar and burn the pieces as a sweet odor to the Lord.
A holocaust of birds may be a turtledove or a young pigeon. The priest twists back the neck and burns the bird on the altar. He does not cut or divide it with metal.
An oblation of fine wheat flour is poured over with oil and set with frankincense. The priest burns a handful with all the frankincense as a memorial, and what remains is for Aaron and his sons.
Every oblation offered to the Lord is made without leaven, and neither leaven nor honey is burned with the sacrifice.

Every sacrifice is seasoned with salt, and the salt of the covenant of God is not taken away. From the first-fruits of grain, still green, a portion is parched, broken, and burned with the oil and all the frankincense.
A sacrifice of peace offerings, from the herd or the flock, male or female, must be immaculate. The one who offers places his hand on its head, and the priests pour the blood all around the altar.
The fat that covers the vital organs, the two kidneys, and the mesh of the liver are burned on the altar as a most sweet odor to the Lord.
By a perpetual law, in every generation and every dwelling, “neither blood nor fat shall you eat at all.”
When the anointed priest sins and the people transgress, he offers an immaculate calf. He sprinkles its blood seven times opposite the veil and puts some on the horns of the altar of incense.

If the whole assembly sins through ignorance, the elders lay their hands on a calf. A leader who sins offers an immaculate he-goat. Someone from the people offers an immaculate she-goat, or a female sheep.
The priest burns the fat on the altar and prays, and the Lord forgives. The rest of the calf is burned beyond the camp, in the clean place where the ashes are poured out.
A witness who hears a voice testifying under oath, and who has seen or knows the matter but does not reveal it, carries his iniquity. Forgotten uncleanness and a forgotten oath also bring guilt.

He offers a female lamb or a she-goat. If he cannot bring a beast, he brings two turtledoves or two young pigeons, one for sin and one for a holocaust. If he cannot bring the birds, he brings a tenth part of an ephah of fine wheat flour, with no oil and no frankincense.
For a mistake about the things sanctified to the Lord, he offers an immaculate ram that can be bought for two shekels, restores the damage, and adds a fifth part more.
Someone who denies a deposit, takes anything by force, accuses falsely, or swears falsely about something he found restores all of it plus a fifth part, and he offers an immaculate ram.
The law of the holocaust: it burns on the altar all night until morning, and the fire on the altar never fails. Each morning the priest places wood under it and burns the fat of the peace offerings.
Aaron and his sons eat the remaining fine flour without leaven in the holy place. A sin offering whose blood is carried into the tabernacle of the testimony is not eaten. It is consumed by fire.
The victim for a transgression is slain where the holocaust is slain, and every male of priestly descent eats it in a holy place. The priest who offers a holocaust keeps its skin.

The flesh of a thanksgiving peace offering is eaten on the same day. What is offered by a vow may still be eaten the next day, but whatever is found on the third day is burned with fire, and eating it nullifies the oblation.
The fat of a sheep, an ox, or a goat is not eaten, and the blood of birds or beasts is not taken as food. The breast that is lifted up and the right shoulder are given to Aaron and his sons.

Moses gathers the assembly, washes Aaron and his sons, and clothes Aaron with the linen undergarment, the wide belt, the hyacinth tunic, the ephod, and the breastplate, on which is Doctrine and Truth.
He anoints the tabernacle and its vessels with the oil of anointing, sprinkles the altar seven times, and pours the oil over Aaron’s head. The calf for sin is burned beyond the camp.

Blood from the ram of consecration is touched to the tip of Aaron’s right ear, the thumb of his right hand, and his foot, and the same is done for his sons. They do not leave the door of the tabernacle for seven days.

On the eighth day Aaron offers an immaculate calf for his own sin and a ram as a holocaust. The people bring a he-goat for sin, a calf and a lamb as a holocaust, and an ox and a ram for peace offerings.

Moses says, “Accomplish it, and his glory will appear to you.” Aaron blesses the people, then Moses and Aaron enter the tabernacle, come out, and bless them, and the glory of the Lord appears to the whole multitude.
A fire from the Lord devours the holocaust and the fat on the altar. The crowd praises the Lord, falling on their faces.

Nadab and Abihu place fire and incense in their censers and offer a strange fire, such as was not instructed of them. Fire coming out from the Lord destroys them, and they die in the sight of the Lord.

Moses says, “I will be sanctified in those who approach me, and I will be glorified in the sight of all the people.” Aaron is silent. The priests are told not to tear their garments, not to leave the tabernacle, and not to drink wine when they enter it.
Moses finds the he-goat for sin burned instead of eaten and is angry with Eleazar and Ithamar. Aaron answers that he could not eat it with a sorrowful mind, and Moses is satisfied.
Whatever has a divided hoof and chews over again may be eaten. The camel, the rock rabbit, the hare, and the swine are unclean.
Of the things that breed in the waters, whatever has fins and scales may be eaten. Among the birds to be avoided are the eagle, the raven, the ostrich, the pelican, and the bat.

The Lord says, “Be holy, for I am Holy.” He says, “For I am the Lord, who led you away from the land of Egypt,” so that he would be their God. The law is given so Israel may know what to eat and what to refuse.
